newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU gears up to deal with telecoms complaints.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU gears up to deal with telecoms complaints.

text.p: The European Commission said on Thursday it had geared up to react swiftly to complaints from companies about national governments that are not opening their telecoms markets to competition.

It said most of the 15 EU countries were doing their best to meet a January 1, 1998 deadline for full telecoms liberalisation, but put the spotlight on laggards including Belgium, Greece, Portugal and Spain.
Using a sports analogy, EU Telecommunications Commissioner Martin Bangemann said those countries were in the "non league", compared with the "premier league" of Britain, Denmark, Finland and Sweden.
"Obviously we're trying to encourage those who are in the non league ... to get a promotion," Bangemann told a news conference.

He and Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, who unveiled a "report card" on implementation of the EU telecoms liberalisation package, said they had set up new internal procedures to monitor the situation.
"We have organised ourselves internally so we can react ad hoc very rapidly if and when problems arise," Van Miert said. "We are expecting complaints to come in."
The report said this would include "expedited recourse" to legal action that could lead to the European Court of Justice.

Van Miert said the Commission was especially concerned about progress in the area of agreements governing "interconnections" between the networks of different telecoms companies, procedures for licensing new operators and the availability of phone numbers.

He said former monopolies can abuse their dominant positions through interconnection agreements, while only about half of the EU states had taken measures needed to ensure there are enough numbers to go around.
Van Miert also singled out Italy for failing to meet a July 1996 deadline for opening its market for telecoms infrastructure to competition.

Italy is in what Bangemann called the "division two" category, along with Austria, Ireland, Italy and Luxembourg. The report said those countries will need to make "considerable efforts" to adopt all measures needed to implement the EU plan.
The "first division" countries include France, Germany and the Netherlands, who have already enacted "wide-ranging measures".

The Commission has agreed that Ireland, Luxembourg, Portugal and Spain can delay liberalisation because they have small or undeveloped networks. It is expected to rule later this month on whether to grant Greece's request to wait until 2003 to introduce full competition.
